page.title: 2 · Sell the inventory
page.description: On-sale queues, pricing, heritage-night offers and giveaway eligibility for an Islanders season. Public facts cited; operational flows and uncited figures are illustrative.

sections.heading: On-sale day: 4,812th in line
text: On a big on-sale, the first problem is traffic, not sales. A waiting room holds thousands of fans and lets them into seat select in batches; when one fan finally gets through, the best seats may already be gone to the presale, and the pair they tap can vanish into someone else's cart.

Facts with a source link: the July 24, 2026 noon on-sale with a priority presale ([NHL.com](https://www.nhl.com/islanders/news/islanders-announce-2026-27-regular-season-schedule)), how Ticketmaster describes its waiting room ([Smart Queue](https://business.ticketmaster.com/smart-queue/)), and the FTC all-in fee rule effective May 12, 2025 ([GRC Report](https://www.grcreport.com/post/ftc-rule-on-unfair-or-deceptive-fees-to-take-effect-on-may-12-2025)). The fan's position, wait times, prices, cart timer and sell-through are illustrative. Seat-map capacities are an illustrative even split of 17,250 seats over 80 sections.
bullets: **Queue** is the hero: one fan joins the waiting room, gets place **4,812** at noon, is let through to seat select, then is held again as two seats in a cart until payment
**Seat map** stays locked (grey, dashed) until the fan is through, then shows presale sell-through, carts and the public wave
**Checkout checks** show the three things that decide the order: all-in price first, card, and whether the seats are still there

steps.text: **11:40 a.m., Friday, July 24.** Single-game tickets for 2026-27 go on sale at noon through Ticketmaster; fans who joined the priority presale list bought earlier. A push tells this fan the waiting room is open. The seat map is locked: nobody picks seats yet.

sections.heading: The pace curve and the member floor
text: A week out, the 300 level is behind pace while the lower bowl runs hot. A price cut can fill it, but only if it does not undercut the season members who paid for those seats in advance, and only if every channel shows the new price. This section walks one game on the UBS Arena map from T-30 to the revenue recap.

Public facts are cited from press and league sources. Ticketing, CRM, app and ad flows are illustrative reconstructions of common industry practice, not descriptions of any team's or vendor's systems. Prices, sales, the pace target and the $31 member per-game price are illustrative; capacities are an even split of 17,250 seats over 80 sections, not venue data. Whether UBS Arena prices dynamically is not verified: this is a generic method on an Islanders-shaped map.
bullets: **Dynamic pricing is not new in hockey.** The SF Giants piloted it with Qcue in 2009, and the Dallas Stars were the first NHL club to follow the same year ([Qcue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qcue), [Sports Illustrated](https://vault.si.com/vault/2009/02/23/tickets-with-flex), [ODU](https://www.odu.edu/news/news-archive/2011/05/ODUProfS_27566)).

**Prices move inside guardrails.** On Ticketmaster, Official Platinum prices are set by the event organizer, such as the team ([Ticketmaster](https://help.ticketmaster.com/hc/en-us/articles/9782440112017-What-are-Official-Platinum-Seats)); the floor and ceiling used here are the author's illustration; the Bruins' flex pricing varies per-game prices for plan holders ([NHL.com](https://www.nhl.com/bruins/tickets/flex-pricing)).

**The member floor** is the guardrail that matters most here: a public seat cheaper than a member's per-game price teaches fans to wait. A fan newsletter made that argument about cheap late tickets in 2024; it is opinion, not data ([Isles Fix](https://www.islesfix.com/p/taking-attendance)).

**All-in prices.** Since May 12, 2025 the FTC fee rule requires the first price shown to include mandatory fees ([GRC Report](https://www.grcreport.com/post/ftc-rule-on-unfair-or-deceptive-fees-to-take-effect-on-may-12-2025)).
Choose **Hold at $38** or **Drop to member floor** below the step controls. Both end on the sold map, with the 300-level revenue in the tiles.

panels.title: UBS Arena · one game, T-30 to T-1 (capacities illustrative)

initial.note: Before T-30. Prices are illustrative: club $165, 100 level $118, 200 level $76, 300 level $38. Capacities are an even split of 17,250 seats, not venue data.

checks.label: All-in price shown first (FTC fee rule)
Ads and email match the price code

steps.text: **T-30.** The weekly pace report lands on the pricing desk. The 100 level is 68% sold and the 200 level 46%, but the 300 level is at 18%. Every number on this map is illustrative.

map.note: T-30 · sold mode: fill = sold ÷ capacity. 100 level 68%, 200 level 46%, 300 level 18% (illustrative).

steps.text: **T-14.** The lower bowl keeps running hot: the 100 level reaches 84%. The 300 level adds only eight points, to 26%, and its end and corner sections are the palest on the map.

map.note: T-14 · 100 level 84%, 200 level 60%, 300 level 26%. Outlined: the slowest 300-level ends and corners.

steps.text: **T-7.** The gap is now the story: the 100 level is 93% sold, the 300 level 33% against an illustrative pace target of 55%. About 3,700 upper-deck seats are unsold with a week to go.

map.note: T-7 · 100 level 93%, 200 level 71%, 300 level 33% (1,858 of 5,590). Illustrative pace target for the 300 level at T-7: 55%.

steps.deltaText: Ticketmaster says Official Platinum prices are set by the event organizer, such as the team; the floor and ceiling here are illustrative guardrails. The FTC fee rule, effective May 12, 2025, requires the first price shown to include mandatory fees. Whether UBS Arena prices dynamically is not verified; this is a generic method.
steps.text: The pricing desk proposes cutting the 300 level from **$38 to $29**. Before it ships, the guardrails run. The CRM returns the member per-game price for the same seats: **$31** (illustrative). The proposal **fails**: a public $29 seat would undercut the season member sitting next to it.

allin.detail: Fees included in the first price the fan sees

approval.detail: Waiting on ticket ops and finance

copy.detail: Ads and email still quote the old price

checks.note: Proposal: 300 level $38 → $29. Blocked by the member floor.

map.note: Proposed: 300 level $38 → $29, all 26 sections. Not applied: the member-floor check failed.

log.text: FAIL member floor: $29 < $31 per-game member price

steps.text: **Hold the price.** The desk withdraws the proposal and keeps $38. Nothing in the channels has to change, so the copy check passes, but the 300 level only creeps to 35% by T-5.

checks.note: Held at $38. Guardrails are not exercised.

steps.text: **T-1: the soft path.** The lower bowl all but sells out, and the 200 level reaches 86%. The 300 level stalls at **41%**: about 3,300 upper-deck seats go unsold, and the building looks thin on camera.

**Recap, held price.** The map stays on sold: the 300 level ends at 41% while the lower bowl carries the night. The tile shows what the upper ring earns: about **$87.7k**. The method is generic: any team can run pace, floor and copy checks this way. Whether UBS Arena prices dynamically is not verified.

map.note: Final, sold mode: 300 level 41% (2,308 of 5,590). Its revenue, ≈ $87.7k at $38, is in the tile (illustrative).

steps.text: **Drop to the member floor.** The desk resubmits at **$31**, equal to the member per-game price. The floor check passes, ops and finance sign off, and the new price code goes live. The map switches to **price mode**: the upper ring pales as its price falls.

floor.detail: $31 = member per-game price; no member undercut

allin.detail: Fees included in the first price shown

approval.detail: Ticket ops and finance signed off

checks.note: 300 level now $31. One check still open.

map.note: Price mode: fill = price ÷ top price ($165 club). 300 level now $31; 100 and 200 levels unchanged.

log.text: PASS member floor · PASS all-in · PASS approval

steps.text: **Channel-sync warning.** Checkout in the fan app shows $31 all-in, but the paid social ads and the reminder email still say **"from $38"**. Fans who see the ad never learn the price fell. By T-5 the 300 level is only at 37%.

allin.detail: Fees included in the first price shown

checks.note: The price changed; the message did not.

map.note: T-5 · sold mode again. 300 level 37% (2,083 of 5,590): barely ahead of the held path.

steps.text: **Marketing pushes new copy.** The ads and a resend to non-buyers now say "upper deck from $31, fees included". The copy check passes, and by T-3 the 300 level reaches 53%.

allin.detail: Fees included in the first price shown

map.note: T-3 · 300 level 53% (2,977 of 5,590) after the copy change.

log.text: PUSH 'from $31, fees included' to ads + email

steps.text: **T-1: the recovery.** The 300 level reaches **72%**, about 1,700 more seats than the held path. The members' $31 still matches the lowest public price, so no member was undercut.

**Recap, member floor.** The map stays on sold: the 300 level ends at 72%. The tile shows about **$125k** against $87.7k on the held path. It multiplies every sold seat by today's price, so the 1,858 seats sold earlier at $38 are counted at $31. The method is generic; UBS Arena dynamic pricing is not verified.

map.note: Final, sold mode: 300 level 72% (4,038 of 5,590). Its revenue, ≈ $125.2k at $31, is in the tile; earlier $38 sales counted at $31 (illustrative).

sections.heading: Two hundred fifty shirts, one link
text: A heritage night looks like a theme on the scoreboard. Underneath, it is a **separate ticket product** with its own link, its own capped item stock and a redemption list tied to barcodes. The Islanders' 2026-27 schedule lists Greek Heritage Night on **Mar 27, 2027 vs Detroit**, with a Greek T-shirt for the *first 250 buyers* ([schedule](https://nhl.com/islanders/tickets/promotional-schedule)). The same pattern ran at the 2024-25 Pride Night on Jan 16, 2025: a belt bag for the first 500 special-ticket buyers ([The Hockey News](https://thehockeynews.com/nhl/new-york-islanders/players/new-york-islanders-promo-nights-group-nights-ubs-arena-release)).
The partner names, codes, clicks, sales and new-to-file counts below are **illustrative**, as are the offer page, CRM and redemption flows. Pick a path to see the shirts sell out or fall short.

bullets.text: **Unique codes per partner** show which community actually brings in *new* fans, not only sales.
**Tie the item count to sales.** Each special-offer ticket reserves one shirt, so the cap is enforced by the sale itself.
**Plan both endings:** offer copy that flips when the item is gone, and a home for leftovers.

panels.title: From partner link to new fan

initial.note: Cap of 250 from the official schedule; 600-seat block illustrative.

steps.text: **Mar 27, 2027 vs Detroit: Greek Heritage Night.** The official schedule lists a Greek T-shirt for the *first 250 buyers* of the special offer ([schedule](https://nhl.com/islanders/tickets/promotional-schedule)). Each partner group gets its own link and code, so every sale can be credited back to the group that sent it.

codes.note: One code each for a parish, a Greek-language school, a cultural society, an alumni chapter, a youth dance troupe and the team email list. All illustrative.

map.note: Outlined: the special-offer block in 212-214 (illustrative). Nothing sold in it yet.

steps.text: Partners post their links in newsletters and group chats. **4,180 clicks** reach the offer page and 3,260 people read past the first screen. Nothing is sold yet, so the shirt count has not moved.

A buyer picks a seat in the special-offer block. Ticketing sells it as its **own SKU**, and each sale reserves **one shirt** in promotions stock. 168 of 820 carts complete, and the budget bar starts its run to 250.

stock.note: One special-offer ticket reserves one shirt. Counts illustrative.

map.note: Special-offer block in 212-214 (illustrative).

steps.text: By early March the count is **204 of 250**. The table already tells the real story: the parish and school links sell most of the seats, while the team's own email list has not been sent.

codes.note: Parish and school codes lead. The team email list has not been sent.

steps.text: **Sells out.** The 250th shirt is reserved two weeks out. Promotions tells the offer page, and the copy must flip to **ticket only, item gone**. A page that still promises a shirt now creates 13 angry buyers at the table.

stock.note: Shirts AT LIMIT. 13 ticket-only sales after the flip. Illustrative.

codes.note: TEAM-EMAIL goes out after the flip, selling ticket-only seats.

steps.text: **Game night.** The redemption table scans each barcode against the list of 250 shirt buyers, not the ticket count. A ticket transferred to a friend still redeems, because the list follows the barcode. 237 shirts go out; 13 are never collected.

stock.note: 263 special-offer seats sold, 250 with a shirt. Illustrative.

map.note: Redemption table placed at 109/110 for illustration.

steps.text: **After the game,** CRM matches every buyer against the file. **118 buyers** have never bought before and are tagged new to file, each with the partner code that brought them in. That column, not total sales, is what the partner program is for.

codes.note: The school code brought in the most new fans per sale. Illustrative.

steps.text: **Surplus.** Sales stall at **221 shirts** in game week. Community relations sends a last-call note through each partner, and the team email list goes out with the shirt still on offer. 29 shirts are unclaimed at puck drop.

stock.note: 29 shirts left at puck drop. Illustrative.

codes.note: TEAM-EMAIL sells 8 in the last week.

steps.text: **Game night.** The table scans barcodes against the list of 221 buyers. 204 shirts go out and 17 buyers never come by, so **46 shirts** are left in the boxes at the end of the night.

stock.note: 221 reserved, 204 picked up at the table. Illustrative.

map.note: Redemption table placed at 109/110 for illustration.

steps.text: **After the game,** the 46 leftover shirts are counted back into promotions stock for the next Greek Heritage Night, so next year's order can be smaller (an illustrative policy). CRM tags **97 new-to-file** buyers by partner code.

stock.note: 221 reserved, 204 picked up: 17 uncollected plus 29 unsold = 46 back to stock. Illustrative.

steps.text: **A theme night is also a set of places.** At the next season's Pride Night, on Mar 26, 2026, the team put a photobooth near **Sec 225** and the Community Relations table, selling Mystery Pucks, at **Secs 109/110** ([NHL.com](https://www.nhl.com/islanders/news/islanders-to-host-pride-night-on-march-26)). The link sells the ticket; fans still have to be sent to the right spot in the building.

map.note: Pulsing: 109/110 and 225, the 2025-26 Pride Night activation spots (Mar 26, 2026).

sections.heading: First 10,000 versus everyone
text: A giveaway rule decides who leaves with the item, how many to order months ahead, and what happens at the gates. Pick a path to run the same illustrative crowd through each rule the Islanders have used: first 10,000, all fans, and a special-offer ticket.

Real nights, items and sponsors are cited on the step markers. Crowd sizes, arrival timing, order sizes and counts are illustrative, and the ticketing, scanning and inventory flow is a reconstruction of common practice, not any team's or vendor's system.

panels.title: UBS Arena · colour = who leaves with the item

initial.note: Colours on this map mean who leaves with the item, not price. Capacities are an illustrative even split of 17,250 seats over 80 sections, not venue data.

checks.label: Every ticket holder can get one
Order size known without a forecast

initial.note: Each path fills these in for its rule. Outcomes are the author's reading, not measured results.

steps.text: One illustrative night at UBS Arena: about **14,200 tickets sold** of 17,250 seats. The lower bowl is nearly full; the 300-level corners and ends are the softest. All three paths reuse this exact crowd, so the only thing that changes between them is the giveaway rule.

map.note: Sold mode: darker = fuller. Sold counts are illustrative.

ledger.note: Tonight, before the giveaway rule is set.

steps.text: The Islanders have used three supply rules in the last two seasons. **First 10,000**: the Mat Barzal bobblehead, Wed Nov 26, 2025. **All fans**: the Ilya Sorokin bobblehead, Fri Nov 27, 2026. **Special offer**: the Italian Heritage T-shirt for the first 500 special-offer buyers, Thu Oct 22, 2026. Before doors open nobody has an item, so the whole bowl is grey.
steps.deltaText: Dates, items, sponsor and rules are from the team schedule and press coverage.

deltaLinks.label: NHL.com: Sorokin and Schaefer bobbleheads for all fans

map.note: Tier mode: here the colour tiers mean who leaves with the item, not price.

ledger.note: Real Islanders nights; links on the step marker.

steps.text: **First 10,000 path.** Promotions sends 10,000 units to the gates, split by each entrance's expected share. The item follows arrival order, not seat location. Half an hour after doors (timing illustrative), early arrivers such as lower-bowl members and club seats have theirs, and most of the building is still grey.

map.note: Shaded per section for readability. Arrival is per person, so real sections are mixed.

steps.text: The 10,000th scan empties the last gate before puck drop (timing illustrative). Lower-bowl and 200-level sideline sections are gold. The 300-level corners and ends, where fans tend to arrive late, stay grey. About **3,100 fans who scanned in go without**.

map.note: Gold: most fans got one. Pale: some did. Grey: mostly missed out. Illustrative.

norace.detail: gates run dry before puck drop

ledger.note: Gate count at the last unit.

steps.text: What the cap buys and what it costs. The order size needs no forecast and every unit is used, and the item pulls people in early. But the night has a "gone" moment at the gates, and the fans who miss out are the ones who came late, not the ones who bought late.

known.detail: fixed at 10,000 when the PO is placed

norace.detail: gates run dry before puck drop

target.detail: goes to early arrivers, whoever they are

sellout.detail: at 17,250 sold, up to 7,250 go without

steps.text: **All fans path.** Every ticket holder gets one, so the whole bowl turns gold. The hard part moves upstream: the order is placed months before the night, so promotions sizes it to the forecast of tickets sold plus a buffer, here 14,100 forecast plus about 4.3%.

map.note: Every section gold: no fan is turned away. Illustrative.

known.detail: needs a sold forecast at the PO

steps.text: Late sales test the buffer. In the final weeks the 300-level corners and ends add about 420 tickets (illustrative), so **14,620 are sold**. The order of 14,700 still covers every ticket, but with only about 80 units to spare. A bigger surge, or a smaller buffer, would have left late fans without one.

map.note: Sold mode: the 300-level corners and ends fill late. Illustrative.

known.detail: needs a sold forecast at the PO

steps.text: Doors: about 13,450 fans scan in (illustrative) and every one gets an item. Nobody races. But the order was sized to tickets sold and no-shows do not collect, so **about 1,250 units are left over** to store, sell or give away later.

map.note: Every section gold. Illustrative.

known.detail: needs a sold forecast at the PO

leftover.detail: ≈1,250 left: sized to sold, handed to scans

soft.detail: order and cost shrink with the crowd

sellout.detail: largest order; forecast error costs either way

steps.text: **Special offer path.** Ticketing creates a separate price code, and partner groups buy through their own link. The item goes to the first 500 buyers of that offer. Here the buyers sit together in 319-322 (seat location illustrative), so only those sections form their own tier; the rest of the bowl gets no item tonight.

map.note: Only special-offer sections are coloured. Seat location illustrative.

steps.text: The stock never goes to the gates. It waits at one pickup table on the concourse (illustrative), where staff check names against the buyer list from ticketing. The other 13,000-plus fans see an ordinary night, and the item count is known the moment the offer sells out.

everyone.detail: not the goal: the item is for offer buyers

early.detail: pickup any time before the end of the night

soft.detail: gives a group a reason to buy

steps.text: Choose the rule from the forecast, not from habit. On a soft weeknight (the lowest reported UBS Arena crowd was 12,739, on a Tuesday in Oct 2024) a first-10,000 cap reaches most fans and gives them a reason to come early. Near a sellout the same cap leaves thousands out, and all fans turns the gate race into a forecasting and cost problem. A special offer can run beside either one.
steps.deltaText: The 12,739 low is reported by a fan newsletter; all other figures here are illustrative.

cells.c: 29 not collected; rest of bowl not offered

steps.text: The change is real. The 2025-26 bobbleheads (Barzal, Bo Horvat) went to the first 10,000; the 2026-27 bobbleheads (Sorokin, Matthew Schaefer) go to all fans, while other 2026-27 items such as the Ford camo hat stay first 10,000. The team has not published a reason, so this section shows only what the change implies for ordering and the gates.
steps.deltaText: The policy change is sourced; the reason for it is not published.

ledger.note: Sourced. Reason for the change: not published.
